name: Onion
listed_description: HTTP server library in C designed to be lightweight and easy to use.
reason: Only performance statement is the README line 'up to 30k web-requests served on a Intel(R) Core(TM)2 Duo CPU T6500 @2.10GHz' for thread-pool epoll mode; no baseline named, no tool, flags or workload. The wiki (26 pages) and repo have no benchmark or comparison with libmicrohttpd, nginx or others. A web search found no third-party shootout including it. Last commit 2022-09-05, 2.1k stars, Apache-2.0 and GPLv2+.

name: PF_RING
reason: README says 'from 80k pkt/sec on a 1,2GHz ARM to more than 20M pkt/sec per core on a low-end 2,5GHz Xeon' and 'enables you to capture packets faster', with no baseline, methodology or benchmark code. doc/*.rst in the dev branch (examples, zc, vanilla, modules) show sample pfcount output only (e.g. 14.2 Mpps / 9.55 Gbps on a ZC interface) and no libpcap comparison. Web search snippets mention PF_RING versus vanilla libpcap comparisons (17% to 58% gains; a Czech MUNI survey and an ISP RAS 2021 paper, plus ntop Cardigliano.pdf and Deri's Ring.pdf), but those hosts (muni.cz, mathnet.ru, ntop.org, luca.ntop.org, edn.com) are blocked in this environment, so nothing could be opened or checked. Worth retrying with open network access: ntop.org PF_RING vs libpcap pages and the 2021 packet-IO frameworks survey. 3.0k stars, GPLv2 kernel and LGPLv2.1 userland, active (dev branch).

name: simple-rpc-cpp
listed_description: A simple RPC wrapper generator to C/C++ functions.
reason: README describes a Python 2 script that generates Boost-serialization RPC wrappers for C/C++ functions so lab equipment SDKs can be called remotely; it contains no benchmark, no speed claim and no comparison with gRPC or any other RPC library.

name: userver
listed_description: Asynchronous C++17 framework with a rich set of abstractions and database drivers for fast and comfortable creation of efficient microservices, services and utilities.
reason: Only comparative evidence is scripts/docs/en/userver/framework_comparison.md, which says userver 'comes ahead of its competitors from the table' in TechEmpower run 3c2e9871-9c2a-4ff3-bc31-620f65da4e74 and shows scripts/docs/img/top15.png: a rank list with userver 13, actix 14, vert.x 15, officefloor 16, drogon 17, vertx-web 18, jooby 19, axum 20. That is ordinal rank only, with no composite scores, requests per second, hardware or flags in the repo, and the techempower.com results page is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), as are Yandex and Medium release posts. The rest of the docs (intro, http_server, pg driver, redis, grpc) carry no speed numbers. Worth retrying with TechEmpower access: composite and per-test scores for userver versus drogon (C++) in that run and in later rounds (Round 23). 3.0k stars, Apache-2.0, active.

name: wdt
listed_description: An embeddedable library (and command line tool) aiming to transfer data between 2 systems as fast as possible over multiple TCP paths.
reason: README 'Performance/Results' gives an internal Facebook figure: 600 Mbytes/sec throttled for RocksDB snapshot transfers, '3x the speed of the previous highly optimized HTTP-based solution', and above 4 Gbytes/sec on a 40 Gbit/s NIC when unthrottled. The baseline is an unnamed internal HTTP-based tool, not a recognizable incumbent such as rsync or scp, and no hardware, code or flags are given for the comparison. The wiki home and FAQ have no numbers (only a note that UDT and BitTorrent were rejected as designs). A web search found no third-party comparison of WDT against rsync, scp, bbcp or FDT (the NSF PAR paper hit is blocked). The repo's own tests (wdt_e2e_test.sh, wdt_max_send_test.sh) only state target throughputs, not baselines.

name: xmlrpc-c
listed_description: A lightweight RPC library based on XML and HTTP.
reason: The project site has performance.php and competitor.php pages (seen in search results) but the host redirects to xmlrpc-c.sourceforge.io, which is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so no numbers could be opened; per the search snippet the performance page compares xmlrpc-c's own server and transport options, not gRPC. The SourceForge svn trunk doc/ directory (COPYING, CREDITS, HISTORY, INSTALL, TESTING, TODO and others) has no benchmark. A search snippet (not opened) about a Perl binding, RPC::Xmlrpc_c versus pure-Perl RPC::XML, mentions CPU-time ratios, but that is a different project. Worth retrying with sourceforge.io access.
